lead: The epistle returns to the passage from 2 Timothy read on New Sunday, and today we stay with its second half: a prisoner whose word is not chained, and a short hymn about dying and living with Christ. The Gospel is the parable of the tenants of the vineyard, which ends with a psalm verse that the first Christians loved: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” Both readings speak of a rejection that God turns into victory.

r.h: The word of God is not chained
set: The writer is a prisoner treated “like a criminal” (2:9), who expects to die soon (4:6). He has just given Timothy three pictures of patient effort, the soldier, the athlete and the farmer, and now asks him to think them over. Then he points to the one memory that makes all effort worthwhile: Jesus Christ, raised from the dead.
str: v. 7: think it over; the Lord will give understanding.
vv. 8–10: remember Christ; Paul in chains; the word not chained; endurance for the sake of the elect.
vv. 11–13: the sure saying, in four lines.
kw: A formula found five times in the Pastoral Letters (1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8). It marks a saying that the Church already knew and trusted, here perhaps part of an early baptismal hymn.
From deō, to bind, the same root as the “chains” (desmoi) that Paul wears. He is bound; the word is not.
The word used for Peter's denial in the Gospels (Mark 14:68, 70). The saying takes it seriously, and then shows that God's faithfulness is greater than ours.
vv: But the word of God is not chained.
Prison walls could hold the apostle but not the Gospel. While he was bound, his letters, his messengers and his example went on.
If we have died with him, we will also live with him;
Most likely a reference to Baptism, in which we die with Christ in order to rise with him (Romans 6:3–8).
if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he will also deny us;
An echo of Jesus' own warning: “whoever denies me before others, I also will deny before my Father in heaven” (Matthew 10:33).
if we are faithless, he remains faithful

Here the pattern of the hymn breaks. We expect “he will be faithless too”. Instead God's faithfulness holds even when ours fails, “for he cannot deny himself”. This does not make denial harmless; verse 12 has just said the opposite. It is the ground of hope for every sinner who comes back.
ch: The Catechism teaches that through Baptism the Christian is plunged into the death of Christ and rises with him (CCC 1227), which is the first line of this hymn. The Church's martyrs, who wrote no letters, proved the second line: their chains became a pulpit, and the word went on.

r.h: The stone that the builders rejected
set: Jesus has entered Jerusalem, cleansed the Temple, and been asked by the chief priests, scribes and elders by what authority he acts (11:27–33). He answers them with this parable, and verse 12 shows that it is aimed at them: “they realized that he had told this parable against them.” The parable concerns the leaders who were responsible for God's vineyard at that time, not the Jewish people as a whole; in fact the crowd protects Jesus here.

The opening words recall Isaiah's song of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7), in which the vineyard is “the house of Israel”. Every listener would have recognized it. In Isaiah the vineyard yields wild grapes; in Jesus' parable the vineyard bears fruit, but the tenants refuse to give it to the owner.
str: v. 1: the owner plants and equips the vineyard and leases it.
vv. 2–5: servant after servant is sent and mistreated.
vv. 6–8: the beloved son is sent last, killed, and thrown out.
v. 9: the owner will give the vineyard to others.
vv. 10–11: Psalm 118: the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone.
v. 12: the leaders understand, and want to arrest him.
kw: The same words the Father spoke at the Baptism (1:11) and the Transfiguration (9:7). In the parable Jesus speaks of himself as the last one sent, and as more than a servant.
Farm workers who rented land and paid the owner part of the harvest, a common arrangement in Jesus' day.
Literally “head of the corner”: either the great foundation stone at the corner, or the stone that crowns an arch or a wall. Either way, the most important stone in the building.
vv: He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’
The owner's hope seems almost foolish. That is the point: God's patience goes beyond what any human owner would show.
So they seized him, killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard.
Hebrews says that Jesus “suffered outside the city gate” (Hebrews 13:12).
The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone;

From Psalm 118:22, a psalm sung at the great pilgrim feasts. In Hebrew there is a play of sound between “son” (ben) and “stone” (’eben), and some commentators think it lies behind the move from parable to psalm. Peter quotes the same verse about the risen Jesus (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7).
ch: The Church reads this parable in the light of Easter: the rejected stone has been raised and made the cornerstone of a new building (CCC 756). The Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in Christ's Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living without distinction, nor against the Jews of today, and that they are not to be presented as rejected by God (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). The parable is a warning for every steward in the Church, in every age, who might treat God's vineyard as his own.

qa: Does verse 9 mean that God has given up on Israel?

No. The parable is addressed to the leaders of that time (12:12), and the vineyard itself is not destroyed; what changes is who tends it. St Paul insists that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29), and the Church teaches that the Jewish people remain dear to God (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839). The warning is for us too: the vineyard is never ours to own.
study: “The word of God is not chained.” Where in my life does the Gospel feel bound or silenced? How might God's word still be at work there?
The tenants wanted the vineyard for themselves. What part of my life, family, work or parish, do I treat as mine rather than as God's, entrusted to me?
